headline: CoffeeZone joins the Riyadh hospitality cluster for the first time
deck: CoffeeZone is new to the Riyadh hospitality cluster this year, arriving with 8,900 branded coffee shops already trading in the Kingdom.
excerpt: CoffeeZone joins the Riyadh hospitality cluster for the first time in 2026, covering a Saudi coffee market the organiser puts at 36 million cups a day and 8,900-plus branded outlets.
content:
CoffeeZone is a new addition to the hospitality cluster opening at Riyadh's convention centre on 15 September, and the figures the organiser attaches to it explain why it has been given its own identity rather than left as an aisle within the hotel supplies hall.

Saudi consumption is put at 36 million cups a day, with more than 8,900 branded coffee shops trading in the Kingdom and a market the organiser projects at $2.27bn by 2033. Whatever the precision of the forecast, the outlet count is the operative number for a trade audience: 8,900 branded sites is an installed base large enough to support a dedicated equipment and consumables supply chain, with its own service networks, distribution and replacement cycles.

Coffee equipment behaves like the hotel kitchen category in miniature, and with one important difference. An espresso machine is capital plant with a service life of several years, specified around a site's expected throughput and difficult to change once the counter is built around it. Unlike most kitchen plant, though, it comes with a continuing consumable relationship attached — beans, and frequently water treatment and servicing — which means the equipment sale is often the beginning of a supply agreement rather than a transaction that closes.

That structure favours suppliers who can offer the whole package, and it is reflected in the participation. Ali Safa of Costa Coffee Professional and Osamah Mohamed Ali Alawwam, founder and managing partner of Roasting House Commercial Company, are both confirmed on the hospitality summit's speaker list, representing the international branded and the domestic roasting sides respectively. The Qatar Specialty Coffee Association appears among the cluster's association partners.

The show's programme is built around competition and demonstration rather than conference sessions — barista and coffee-art competitions, live brewing and espresso demonstrations, and workshops, with the Saudi Arabia Barista Championship hosted at the event. That format suits a category where the purchase decision involves tasting the output and watching the machine work, which is not true of most equipment sold at trade exhibitions.

For the hotel audience the cluster is aimed at, coffee sits inside a larger question about food and beverage as a revenue line. Hotel F&B has historically been a cost centre justified by guest expectation rather than a profit centre in its own right, and operators across the region have been reworking that assumption — which is why food and beverage as a growth driver appears as a declared theme of the adjoining hospitality summit.

The market figures here are the organiser's own and should be attributed as such; no independent verification of the 36 million cup or 8,900 outlet numbers was available.
